item.title: Version 2.0
item.description:
• The island is the notch, grown. While you talk, a deep black shape comes out of the notch itself, with the waveform, a live dot, and your words settling in below it: white once they have held steady, mint for a word the engine went back and changed, dim for what it only just heard. On a Mac without a notch it hangs from the menu bar.
  • Dictation starts in about a twentieth of a second. Slate now opens the Mac’s own microphone directly instead of asking the system for whatever input is selected. With AirPods on, that used to mean waiting up to a second and a half for the Bluetooth call profile, and your music dropping to call quality; now the AirPods are never touched. There is a switch in Settings if you would rather use the headset’s microphone.
  • Real paragraphs. Pause for a beat and the next thing you say starts a new paragraph. And when your cursor already sits after text on a line, the words begin on a fresh paragraph instead of running into it.
  • Glass. The welcome card and the picker sit on Liquid Glass on macOS 26.
  • Sounds you can choose. Classic (the soft Pop and Tink as before), Soft, Marimba, Click, or Off, in Settings.
  • Tap-to-stop lands its words. A Cmd-V is never sent while a modifier key is still held down.

item.title: Version 1.2.3
item.description:
• The microphone comes back after you change headphones. Unplugging a headset and going back to the Mac's own microphone could leave Slate unable to find any input at all — not for a moment, but until you quit and reopened it. The talk key looked fine and simply did nothing. Slate now recovers from a microphone that stops answering, instead of giving up on it for the rest of the session.
  • A microphone that quietly went away is noticed. If the device Slate is holding disappears, it no longer trusts that the microphone is still there: it rebuilds on whatever input you have now, rather than opening the panel over a dead microphone and hearing nothing you say.
  • Pressing the talk key right after a device change works. Swapping audio devices leaves a moment where macOS reports no microphone at all. Slate used to take that as final and fail the dictation; it now waits the moment out, which is all it ever needed.

item.title: Version 1.2.2
item.description:
• The picker opens on the last thing you dictated. Press ⌘ with your talk key and what you just said is the first row, already selected — so putting it somewhere else is the shortcut and Return, nothing more. Saved notes sit underneath it, and older dictations below those.
  • A one-press fix when the talk key loses its permission. macOS ties Accessibility to how an app is signed, and an update can leave a row that still looks switched on but no longer counts — the talk key stops with nothing on screen to explain it. Slate now offers Repair in the menu, in Settings, on the setup page and on the launch card: it asks first, then removes its own entry and has macOS ask again. No more taking the row out and adding it back by hand.
  • Fewer false alarms about that permission. Just after you log in, macOS can report a perfectly good permission as missing while it is busy answering everyone at once. Slate used to believe that instantly — a card claiming the talk key was off, and a dictation cancelled mid-sentence if the blip landed while you were speaking. It now waits for the answer to settle before saying or doing anything about it.
  • A dictation can no longer hang on the speech engine. 1.2.1 gave the microphone a deadline; transcription had none, so a system service that stopped answering could leave your words stuck in the island with no way out. It now has thirty seconds, which is dozens of times the longest real transcription. Downloading a speech model is deliberately exempt, so switching language mid-sentence still finishes however long it takes.

item.title: Version 1.2.1
item.description:
• A fix for Slate freezing solid. When the Mac's own audio system stops answering — it can happen after heavy use, a headphone switch, or a long call — Slate used to freeze with it: the icon stopped responding, and the talk key went dead, sometimes for minutes. Slate now asks for the microphone off to the side and gives the system five seconds. If the answer never comes, that one dictation shows a message and everything else keeps working; the moment the Mac's audio recovers, Slate does too.
  • A dictation that started slowly is never thrown away. A slow microphone start could make a long hold read as an accidental tap, and the words disappeared with nothing said about it. The hold is now measured from your press, and if the microphone truly never opened, Slate tells you nothing was heard instead of staying quiet.

item.title: Version 1.2.0
item.description:
• Say a thought without typing it. Hold Shift with the talk key and Slate keeps the words instead of putting them in the app you are in. A separate key opens a short list of your newest notes and your last few dictations, and the one you pick is typed at your cursor. Notes stay on this Mac until you delete them, and Settings has the full list.
  • Dictate a numbered list and get one. Say "one, milk, two, eggs, three, bread" and it comes out as a list. If the pauses are not landing where you want them, say the word "comma" between the parts instead and it works every time.
  • A list only happens when you meant one. Counting, quantities, prices, clock times, decimals and version numbers all stay as ordinary sentences.

item.title: Version 1.1.7
item.description:
• Setup is five short steps, and it waits for the microphone and Accessibility instead of letting you past them. Skipping those was how Slate ended up installed and silent, with the talk key doing nothing and no explanation on screen.
  • Setup also shows you the dictionary and the history, which people were only finding by accident.
  • Spoken single quotes. Say “apostrophe” and “close apostrophe” around something and you get the marks, and “quote … unquote” works too.
  • A new setting keeps the last dictation on the clipboard, so you can paste it again yourself. It is off unless you turn it on.
  • The speech model downloads in the background while you set Slate up, rather than making you wait on a screen of its own.

item.title: Version 1.1.6
item.description:
• Saying “new paragraph” or “new line” works again after an ordinary phrase. In 1.1.5 a sentence like “Thanks for the update new paragraph…” typed the words out instead of making the break.
  • Saying “scratch that” in the middle of a sentence works again, and spoken email addresses join again.
  • A hands-free session ends on silence again instead of staying open.
  • If the speech model fails to load, pressing the talk key now retries properly instead of showing the same message every time.
  • Dictating twice in a row no longer repeats the last few words of the first take.

item.title: Version 1.1.5
item.description:
• Typing a character that needs the Right Option key, like the @ sign on a Spanish or German keyboard, no longer starts a recording. It also no longer throws away the sentence you had just finished.
  • Clipboard history apps like Maccy, Paste, and Alfred no longer keep a copy of everything you dictate. Slate now marks the text so those apps skip it.
  • Several cleanup rules were taking out words they should have left alone. "A brand new line of products" and "the very next line" stay as words. "Bora Bora" and "Duran Duran" keep both halves. Saying "scratch that" after a spoken paragraph break no longer reaches back too far.
  • Quiet speech is no longer cut off part way through a long sentence.
  • Cleanup runs faster, so your words land sooner after you let go of the key.

item.title: Version 1.1.4
item.description:
• The talk key starts at once. Slate keeps the microphone ready for a minute after you speak, so talking again does not wait for it to warm up. There is a switch for this in Settings under Speed.
  • The green marks in the live text now only appear on a word Slate went back and changed its mind about. They used to appear on words that had simply moved along the line.
  • Time saved counts the time you actually spent speaking, measured, instead of assuming everyone speaks at the same pace.

item.title: Version 1.1.3
item.description:
• When the talk key stops working, Slate now says so. The menu bar icon changes, and the menu tells you how to put it back.
  • Putting it back has a step that is easy to miss, so Slate spells it out: if Slate is already in the Accessibility list, take it out and add it again.
  • The welcome card no longer sits against the camera notch.

item.title: Version 1.1.2
item.description:
• Changing headphones mid sentence no longer cuts your words short. Slate waits for the new microphone and keeps going.
  • If the microphone does go away for good, Slate types what it heard instead of leaving the pill on screen.
  • Quitting Slate while your music is paused now starts the music again.

item.title: Version 1.1.1
item.description:
• New spoken commands: full stop, semicolon, next paragraph, closed brackets, and curly braces.
  • Adding words to the dictionary is simpler: say it on the left, get it on the right, press Return.
  • The setup card stays clear of the camera cutout, can be closed, and opens System Settings only once.
  • Anything dictated into a password field stays out of history.
  • Steadier long dictations, quicker auto-stop, and dozens of small fixes.

item.title: Version 1.1.0
item.description: • Slate can now update itself. The switch is in Settings › About, and it stays off until you turn it on.
